title: Why suffering?
hookLine: the Qur'an promises tests, and tells a story about a wisdom that only shows up later

cards: "And surely We shall try you with something of fear and hunger, and loss of wealth and lives and crops; but give glad tidings to the steadfast." That's the Qur'an, in Pickthall's translation.
It doesn't promise an easy life; it promises tests. The next verse describes the steadfast: when misfortune strikes them, they say, "Lo! we are Allah's and lo! unto Him we are returning."
Muslims say it at news of a death or a loss. The theologians argued long about why a just and merciful God allows pain.

teach.b: You met the Qur'an's clearest picture on day 468: Musa and al-Khidr, in Surah al-Kahf.
Musa travels with a servant of Allah given knowledge from Him; tradition calls him al-Khidr. Musa asks to learn from him, and is warned he won't be able to bear it. Then three strange things happen.
Al-Khidr makes a hole in the boat of poor people who gave them a ride. He kills a boy. And in a town that refused them food, he rebuilds a falling wall and asks nothing for it.
Each time Musa protests, and each time he's reminded of the warning. At the parting, al-Khidr explains. A king was seizing every boat by force; a damaged one might be passed over.
The boy would have burdened his believing parents with rebellion and disbelief. The wall hid treasure belonging to two orphans, and it had to stand until they were grown.
What Musa saw as harm had a purpose he couldn't see. And another verse: "Allah knoweth, ye know not." That doesn't make pain small, and Islam doesn't ask anyone to pretend it is.
When the Prophet Muhammad's ﷺ son Ibrahim was dying, Sahih al-Bukhari records that his eyes filled with tears.

He said the eye weeps and the heart grieves, and we say only what pleases our Lord. A hadith in Sahih Muslim says the believer's affair is all good: thankful in ease, patient in hardship, and both bring good.
It doesn't say every loss makes sense today. The story of the boat says the wisdom is not always seen.

how: Muslims meet hardship with patience, sabr, and say "we are Allah's and unto Him we are returning" at news of a death or loss; grief and tears are not forbidden, and the Prophet himself wept.

o: the idea that pain always means you've been punished for sins
the Qur'an's tests, patience, and a wisdom not always seen
a teaching that true faith should keep you from ever crying

p: a king was seizing every boat

s: in Islam, patience means never crying
Sahih al-Bukhari records the Prophet weeping at the death of his son Ibrahim.
the Qur'an promises believers a life without hardship
it says We shall try you with fear, hunger and loss.
Musa understood al-Khidr's actions only when he explained them
each time Musa protested; the reasons came at the parting.

games.q: you're Musa. your guide has just made a hole in the boat of the poor people who gave you a ride. what do you do?
games.why: Musa protests, though he'd promised patience. Later he learns a king was seizing every boat by force, and a damaged one might be passed over.

practice: Let one hard thing come to mind, not the hardest, one you can hold for two minutes, and don't hurry to explain it; if grief comes, let it come, the Prophet wept.
Then set one more thought beside the question, without pushing it away: I may not see all of it.
If you pray, say, unto Him we are returning; and if a loss feels too heavy to carry alone, in the US call or text 988, any hour, or elsewhere, local emergency help.

wordCard.voice: Why suffering? The Qur'an speaks of tests, of patience, and of a wisdom not always seen, told in the story of Musa and al-Khidr. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: not always seen. Tears and trust, side by side, in the same breath. Rest well.
